subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: In which file organization are records stored one after another, and reading record N requires scanning all previous records?
explanation: Sequential files store records in order; access is inherently serial. Indexed files use an index for faster lookup; direct uses hashing for O(1) access.

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: A primary index is built on:
option_a: The ordering key field of a sorted file
explanation: A primary index is constructed on the key/ordering field of a sequentially sorted data file; secondary indexes use other fields.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: Why are B+ trees preferred over binary search trees for database indexes on disk?
option_a: Their high fan-out reduces tree height, so far fewer disk accesses are needed
option_c: They are always stored in memory
explanation: Wide B+ tree nodes (many keys per node) keep depth small (typically 3-4 levels), minimizing slow disk I/O, and leaves are linked for range scans.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: In RAID terminology, what does 'striping' mean?
option_a: Splitting data across multiple disks in blocks to improve throughput
option_b: Copying identical data to every disk
explanation: Striping distributes data across disks so reads/writes can happen in parallel. Mirroring duplicates data for redundancy.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: RAID 0 (striping) offers which property?
option_a: Better performance but no fault tolerance
explanation: RAID 0 stripes data for speed but has zero redundancy - one failed disk loses all data on the array.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: RAID 1 (mirroring) with 2 disks provides:
option_a: Fault tolerance - data survives one disk failure, at the cost of 50% usable capacity
explanation: Mirroring writes the same data to both disks: read performance improves and one disk can fail without data loss, but capacity is halved.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: RAID 5 uses distributed parity. What is the minimum number of disks required and how many disk failures can it survive?
explanation: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across 3+ disks; it tolerates a single disk failure and rebuilds from parity.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: Which RAID level tolerates two simultaneous disk failures using double distributed parity?
explanation: RAID 6 stores two parity blocks per stripe (minimum 4 disks) and survives up to two disk failures. RAID 10 mirrors striped sets.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: RAID 10 (1+0) combines which two techniques?
explanation: RAID 10 mirrors then stripes: performance of striping plus fault tolerance of mirroring; needs 4 disks minimum and can lose one disk per mirror pair.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: Which backup strategy copies only files changed since the last FULL backup?
option_a: Incremental (relative to full) - depends on definition
option_c: Mirroring to a second site only
explanation: A differential backup captures all changes since the last full backup, growing each time; incremental captures changes since the last backup of any type.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: Which is generally the fastest and most common primary/secondary trade-off for a database server's working data?
option_a: NVMe SSD for hot data, HDD/object storage for cold/archival data
option_b: Magnetic tape for all online queries
explanation: Tiered storage matches media to access: flash for performance-sensitive data, HDD/tape/object stores for capacity and archival.
source: PGIMER CP-047 prep bank - original practice (Batch 1)

subject: Storage / RAID / Data Organization
question: When choosing a RAID level, the fundamental trade-off is between:
option_a: Capacity/performance versus redundancy/fault tolerance (and rebuild cost)
option_b: RAM size and CPU speed only
explanation: More redundancy (parity/mirroring) consumes capacity and write bandwidth; striping without redundancy maximizes space/speed but risks data loss.
